title: Trial Endpoints for Candidemia and Invasive Candidiasis: Consensus Recommendations by the Mycoses Study Group Education & Research Consortium and European Confederation of Medical Mycology.
sourceName: Clinical infectious diseases : an official publication of the Infectious Diseases Society of America
abstract: Invasive candidiasis (IC) remains the most common invasive mycosis world-wide, responsible for a wide range of infections that can range from superficial mucosal infections to life-threatening systemic diseases. Clinical trials of antifungal agents for IC are pivotal to its management. Therapeutic responses in these trials are currently based on consensus criteria initially presented by the Mycoses Study Group (MSG) and the European Organization for Research and the Treatment of Cancer (EORTC) in 2008. These 2008 definitions originally described by Segal et al are still employed by both investigators and regulatory agencies when evaluating antifungal drug efficacy and patient outcomes. However, advances in clinical mycology, the change in epidemiology of Candida infections due to the increase in non-albicans Candida species, and the increase in newer antifungal agents currently under development require a revision of these criteria to ensure appropriate and standardized adjudication of patient outcomes and to accurately capture responses to newer therapeutic regimens and modern interventions. Therefore, the European Confederation of Medical Mycology (ECMM) and Mycoses Study Group Education and Research Consortium (MSGERC) have decided to revise the criteria to be used for future studies.

abstract: Invasive fungal diseases remain a significant cause of patient morbidity and mortality. Outcome evaluation in most mycology clinical trials is currently based on consensus criteria published in 2008. However, advances in diagnosis and management of various mycoses and the ever-expanding population of patients at risk necessitate a revision and refinement of these criteria. Appropriate categorization of antifungal treatment response is crucial in assessing the effects of new therapeutic interventions. An international expert panel nominated by the European Confederation of Medical Mycology (ECMM) and Mycoses Study Group Education and Research Consortium (MSGERC) was convened to update the current outcome evaluation criteria. The panel achieved consensus on updated guidelines for assessing treatment responses and defining study outcomes in clinical trials of aspergillosis and other mold diseases, invasive candidiasis, cryptococcosis, and dimorphic fungi in both adults and children. title: Candidalysin: a decade of discovery.
abstract: Candida albicans is a globally prevalent commensal fungus and a major pathogen of humans that causes both superficial infections and lethal disease. Identifying the biological mechanisms that advance our understanding of C. albicans colonization and pathogenicity, and that may lead to disease prevention, is of critical importance. A decade ago, C. albicans was found to secrete a peptide toxin called candidalysin, the first of its kind produced by a human fungal pathogen. Here we review the first decade of candidalysin research and focus on the critical function that candidalysin plays in commensalism, infection and disease. Specifically, we discuss its role as a classical virulence factor, how it activates host immune responses in different disease models and its emerging role as a commensal factor in the gut microbiota. We outline how this decade of discovery is facilitating the development of therapeutics and what research questions are waiting to be answered.

abstract: This is a phase 1b/2 study of a single dose of intravenous (IV) bacteriophage in males and non-pregnant females, at least 18 years old, diagnosed with Cystic Fibrosis (CF). title: Isavuconazole in the management of central nervous system fungal infections: Parenchymal penetration and clinical performance.
abstract: Invasive fungal infections (IFIs) involving the central nervous system (CNS) represent a critical challenge, with mortality of 50% or more in cerebral aspergillosis, mucormycosis, fusariosis and cryptococcal meningitis, and pharmacokinetic (PK) access restricted by the blood-brain barrier (BBB). This review analyzes the clinical performance and parenchymal penetration of isavuconazole (ISA), a second-generation triazole. ISA exhibits linear PK, a cyclodextrin-free intravenous formulation, and high tissue affinity, favored by moderate lipophilicity (experimental logP 2.56) and in vitro inhibition of P-glycoprotein and breast cancer resistance protein (BCRP) efflux transporters. Experimental evidence from animal models shows brain-to-plasma ratios of 0.42 to 1.8, indicating efficient BBB crossing. Human biopsy data show a fundamental PK dichotomy. While cerebrospinal fluid concentrations are restricted (about 1% of plasma), levels in fungal abscesses and inflamed parenchyma reach up to 5.11 mg/L, exceeding the minimum inhibitory concentration reported for Aspergillus fumigatus in those cases. Clinically, ISA was associated with a response in 70% of first-line (n = 10) and 73% of salvage-treated patients (n = 30) with cerebral aspergillosis, and 82% of 28 patients with CNS-only coccidioidomycosis improved or stabilized. Meta-analyses suggest fewer drug-related adverse events and, in randomized subgroups, fewer hepatobiliary events compared with voriconazole, although moderate cytochrome P450 3A4 inhibition warrants monitoring of calcineurin and mechanistic target of rapamycin (mTOR) inhibitors in transplant recipients. ISA is a strategic option for high-complexity CNS-involving IFIs, serving as a therapeutic alternative in salvage and prolonged-maintenance settings, though first-line use in CNS infection awaits confirmation from randomized trials. Central nervous system fungal infections are hard to treat because few drugs reach the affected tissue. This review shows that isavuconazole, a second-generation extended-spectrum azole, penetrates brain tissue and is linked to clinical responses, although the evidence is mostly retrospective.

title: Clinicobacteriological profile, Mortality Predictors and Antimicrobial Resistance in Necrotising Soft Tissue Infections: A prospective study.
abstract: BACKGROUND: Necrotising soft tissue infections (NSTIs) are rapidly progressive infections requiring prompt diagnosis and management. This study assessed predictors of mortality, microbiological spectrum, antimicrobial resistance patterns, and differences between polymicrobial and monomicrobial NSTIs in a prospective manner. METHODS: This study enrolled patients aged 15 years or older with clinically suspected NSTIs who presented between March 2022 and February 2023. Clinical, laboratory, surgical, and outcome data were collected. Tissue and pus samples were processed for aerobic and anaerobic cultures. Antimicrobial susceptibility testing was performed according to CLSI guidelines. Mortality-associated factors were analysed using univariate analysis, binary logistic regression, and survival analysis. RESULTS: Eighty-seven patients were included, predominantly male (87.3%), with a median age of 47.5 years. Extremities were most commonly affected. The mortality rate of this cohort was 25.3%. Polymicrobial infections predominated (49.4%), while monomicrobial NSTIs were associated with higher mortality (p = 0.022). Gram-negative organisms, particularly Acinetobacter baumannii and Escherichia coli, were the most frequent pathogens. Obligate anaerobes were significantly associated with polymicrobial infections. Chronic liver disease (p = 0.003) and systemic toxicity (p = 0.018) independently predicted mortality, whereas higher haemoglobin levels were protective. High antimicrobial resistance was observed, including carbapenem-resistant A. baumannii and Enterobacterales. Among the anaerobes, resistance to clindamycin and cefoxitin, along with reduced susceptibility to metronidazole, was reported. CONCLUSION: NSTIs remain associated with substantial mortality, especially in monomicrobial infections due to multidrug-resistant Gram-negative pathogens. Early recognition, prompt surgery, and region-specific empirical antimicrobial therapy are crucial for improving outcomes.

title: Farm-originated Antimicrobial Resistance Modeling: Exploring Humans-to-Animal Dissemination
abstract: Antimicrobial resistance is a major public health issue. Methicillin resistance in Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA) is one of the indicators that is monitored particularly closely. In animals, pig farms, among others, have been identified as reservoirs of MRSA, with a risk of transmission to humans, particularly to individuals in direct contact with livestock. In France, the prevalence of MRSA in pig farms has increased markedly in recent years. While cross-species transmission between pigs and humans in professional settings is well-documented, the temporal dynamics, the actual incidence of acquisition, and the associated determinants remain insufficiently characterized in France. Adopting a "One Health" approach, this project aims to gain a better understanding of the mechanisms by which MRSA spreads between animal and human subpopulations and to incorporate these insights into a mathematical modeling framework.

title: The evolution of carbapenem-resistant Klebsiella pneumoniae in Greek intensive care units is driven by local carbapenemase acquisition, nationwide nosocomial spread and emerging resistance to novel antimicrobials.
abstract: OBJECTIVES: We investigated transmission patterns and therapeutic options for Carbapenem-resistant Klebsiella pneumoniae (CR-Kp) in Greek ICUs. METHODS: CR-Kp isolates (N=271) were prospectively collected from patients in 17 Greek ICUs between 2021-2023 (INCREASE study, funded by Pfizer). Susceptibility profiles were determined by broth microdilution and genomes sequenced with Oxford Nanopore. RESULTS: All isolates produced carbapenemases: 48% KPC, 20% NDM, 4.4% VIM, 27.6% multi-carbapenemase producers. Resistance to carbapenems, fluoroquinolones, aminoglycosides, and co-trimoxazole exceeded 90%, except for amikacin (73.4%) and colistin (46.5%). Aztreonam-avibactam and cefepime-zidebactam showed the highest susceptibility, 94.5% and 91.6% respectively, yet resistance was >10% among multi-carbapenemase producers. High levels of resistance to cefiderocol (41.7%) and cefepime-taniborbactam (21.4%) were detected. Aztreonam-avibactam resistance co-occurred with VEB-25 and a novel VEB variant. Predominant sequence types included ST39 (28.1%), ST11 (22.7%), and ST258 (18.4%). Time-scaled phylogenies demonstrated that following CG importation CR-Kp often acquired multiple carbapenemases. Over 88% of isolates were implicated in transmission clusters involving 1-8 ICUs across the country. CONCLUSIONS: In Greek ICUs, CR-Kp appears to emerge via local plasmid acquisition and then spread within and between hospitals. While aztreonam-avibactam and cefepime-zidebactam remain promising treatment options, resistance among multi-carbapenemase producers and diagnostic gaps (notably for VEB variants) are concerning.

abstract: BACKGROUND: Independently evaluated population pharmacokinetic models and clinically derived pharmacokinetic/pharmacodynamic targets for colistin sulfate remain limited. Plasma concentrations were measured by validated ultra-performance liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry. Modeling used nonlinear mixed-effects modeling software (NONMEM). Logistic regression and receiver operating characteristic (ROC) analysis assessed efficacy predictors and the exploratory threshold. title: The burden of bacterial antimicrobial resistance in the South Asia and high-income Asia-Pacific region over three decades: a systematic analysis.
abstract: BACKGROUND: Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) is an escalating global public health crisis, yet regional disparities remain poorly characterized. This study systematically assessed AMR burden in South Asia and High-income Asia-Pacific (1990-2021) to inform targeted control strategies. METHODS: We analyzed data from the Global Burden of Antimicrobial Resistance Study 2021, which serves as the most advanced and current database for assessing the burden of AMR. The study covered 22 pathogens, 84 pathogen-drug combinations, and 11 infectious syndromes in countries and territories across South Asia and High-income Asia-Pacific regions. We quantified the deaths burden under two counterfactual scenarios: deaths associated with AMR and deaths attributable to AMR. In addition, based on these data, we calculated the estimated annual percentage change (EAPC) to evaluate the temporal trends in AMR death rate. RESULTS: In 2021, South Asia recorded approximately 1.26 million (95% UI: 1.11 to 1.42 million) AMR-associated deaths and 334,671 (95% UI: 282,451 to 386,890) AMR-attributable deaths, while the High-income Asia-Pacific region reported 108,668 (95% UI: 92,005 to 125,331) and 23,717 (95% UI: 20,074 to 27,360). abstract: RATIONALE: Cavitary lung cancer, particularly squamous cell carcinoma (SCC), can closely mimic infectious cavitary diseases such as pulmonary aspergillosis. When molecular pathogen testing yields a positive result, the infectious diagnosis may be erroneously reinforced, and histological confirmation may be delayed. PATIENT CONCERNS: A 68-year-old male farmer with a 40 pack-year smoking history presented with a 6-month history of cough, expectoration, and chest tightness. Chest computed tomography revealed a 66 mm × 70 mm thick-walled cavitary lesion in the left upper lobe. Targeted next-generation sequencing of bronchoalveolar lavage fluid at the referring hospital detected Aspergillus flavus sequences, leading to a misdiagnosis of pulmonary aspergillosis and 2.5 months of voriconazole therapy, during which the lesion progressed. DIAGNOSES: Repeat bronchoscopy at our institution revealed a fistulous opening with intracavitary nodules and necrotic material. Endobronchial ultrasound-guided transbronchial needle aspiration (EBUS-TBNA) at stations 4 L and 10 L confirmed poorly differentiated lung SCC. 18F-fluorodeoxyglucose positron emission tomography/computed tomography (PET-CT) demonstrated hypermetabolism in the primary lesion, mediastinal lymph nodes, and sternum, supporting a clinical-radiological diagnosis of stage IVA (cT4N2M1b) disease. INTERVENTIONS: The patient received first-line paclitaxel plus carboplatin combined with tislelizumab for 6 cycles, followed by tislelizumab maintenance monotherapy. OUTCOMES: A partial response according to the Response Evaluation Criteria in Solid Tumors version 1.1 was achieved after the first cycle, with sustained tumor shrinkage after 6 cycles and no evidence of disease progression during ongoing maintenance therapy. LESSONS: In cavitary lung lesions, targeted next-generation sequencing detection of fungal sequences should not by itself override the need for histological evaluation, because molecular assays cannot distinguish colonization or contamination from invasive infection. Endobronchial ultrasound-guided transbronchial needle aspiration combined with positron emission tomography/computed tomography is valuable for diagnosis and staging when cavitary malignancy is suspected, and SCC remains an important subtype of cavitary lung cancer in long-term smokers.

title: Research advances and clinical management of drug interactions between voriconazole and antituberculosis agents.
abstract: BACKGROUND: When tuberculosis is complicated by fungal infection, voriconazole and antituberculosis drugs may need to be used in combination, and drug interactions can affect efficacy and safety. METHODS: This structured narrative review used a systematic literature search of PubMed, Embase, Web of Science, and the China National Knowledge Infrastructure (CNKI) from database inception to May 2026, together with predefined eligibility criteria and evidence stratification. Clinical pharmacokinetic, therapeutic drug monitoring (TDM), observational, case-report, and case-series studies were eligible as the primary evidence base. Relevant RESULTS: A total of 2,198 records were identified, and 17 primary clinical studies were included. Most were case reports or small retrospective studies, with limited paired antituberculosis-drug exposure data and clinical outcomes; generalizability is therefore limited. Existing clinical pharmacokinetic evidence is concentrated on rifamycins. Rifampicin markedly reduces voriconazole exposure and its induction may persist after discontinuation, so coadministration should be avoided. Rifapentine can also substantially lower voriconazole concentrations, with interindividual variability in the offset of induction; dose adjustment and re-initiation after withdrawal require serial TDM. Rifabutin has a bidirectional interaction: it can reduce voriconazole exposure, while voriconazole may increase exposure to rifabutin and its active metabolite. Current U.S. voriconazole labeling lists rifabutin coadministration as contraindicated, and rare off-label case experience does not establish it as a safe alternative. For isoniazid, ethambutol, linezolid, and other non-rifamycin agents, available evidence is mechanistic or hypothesis-generating and does not establish causal interactions or justify empirical voriconazole dose adjustment. CONCLUSION: Management should prioritize avoidance of voriconazole coadministration with rifampicin and rifabutin in accordance with current labeling, and avoidance of rifapentine where feasible. If rifapentine exposure cannot be avoided or has recently stopped, serial TDM should guide voriconazole dosing. For non-rifamycin antituberculosis drugs, monitoring should be matched to the suspected risk (exposure variability, QT prolongation, hepatotoxicity, or optic, neurologic, or hematologic toxicity) rather than based on unvalidated empirical dose changes.

title: Drug Dosing During Continuous Renal Replacement Therapy in Critically Ill Patients: A Practical Narrative Review.
abstract: Drug dosing during continuous renal replacement therapy (CRRT) is difficult in critically ill patients because drug exposure is influenced by both the patient and the extracorporeal treatment. This narrative review provides a practical overview of drug dosing during CRRT, while intermittent hemodialysis and sustained low-efficiency dialysis are discussed only where they provide relevant contextual or comparative information. It summarizes the main drug-related, patient-related, and treatment-related factors that influence extracorporeal drug clearance and discusses their clinical implications for commonly used drug classes. Loading and maintenance doses should be considered separately: loading doses depend mainly on volume of distribution and the need for early therapeutic exposure, whereas maintenance dosing depends on total clearance, including residual renal, extracorporeal, and non-renal clearance. Therapeutic drug monitoring can help guide dose adjustment when validated targets are available, while model-informed precision dosing may provide additional support in selected patients. The review also proposes an eight-step practical framework based on residual kidney function, the actual delivered CRRT prescription, drug pharmacokinetics and pharmacodynamics, therapeutic monitoring, and repeated reassessment. Future approaches may combine real-time CRRT data with pharmacokinetic models to support more individualized dosing.

title: Dynamic Radiologic Severity Index is associated with antifungal treatment but does not independently predict initiation in pediatric acute lymphoblastic leukemia with post-chemotherapy pneumonia.
abstract: BACKGROUND: Invasive fungal pneumonia remains a diagnostic challenge in immunocompromised children with acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL), as conventional microbiological tests have limited sensitivity. This retrospective study evaluated whether serial chest computed tomography (CT) scored with the Radiologic Severity Index (RSI) was associated with initiation of antifungal therapy in 87 children with ALL and chemotherapy-related pneumonia. METHODS: A retrospective analysis was conducted on 87 pediatric patients [median age 6.2 years, interquartile range (IQR) 3.5-8.0 years] diagnosed with ALL who developed pneumonia during chemotherapy between March 2016 and October 2024. Demographic data, medical history, and laboratory findings were collected for each patient. Chest CT images were assessed using the RSI, which quantifies affected lung volume and regional opacity (range 0-48). Clinical and radiologic characteristics of fungal and non-fungal pneumonia cases were compared using t-tests, Mann-Whitney U tests, Pearson's Chi-squared tests, or Fisher's exact tests. Additionally, binary logistic regression models were employed to examine the correlation between RSI and antifungal therapy initiation. RESULTS: No significant differences in baseline or peak RSI were observed between fungal and non-fungal groups, nor between antifungal-treated and untreated groups (all P>0.05). Routine laboratory parameters, including leukocyte, neutrophil, and lymphocyte counts, as well as serum albumin levels, did not differ between groups (all P>0.05). However, the antifungal-treated group demonstrated significantly higher change from baseline to peak Radiologic Severity Index (ΔRSI) (P=0.01) and RSI variation rate (P=0.02) compared to the untreated group. In multivariable logistic regression adjusted for potential confounders, neither ΔRSI [odds ratio (OR) =1.14, 95% confidence interval (CI): 0.94-1.37, P=0.18] nor RSI variation rate (OR =0.54, 95% CI: 0.15-1.98, P=0.36) emerged as an independent predictor of antifungal therapy initiation. CONCLUSIONS: Dynamic RSI metrics (ΔRSI and RSI variation rate) are significantly elevated in pediatric ALL patients with chemotherapy-related pneumonia who receive antifungal therapy, whereas static RSI metrics and routine laboratory parameters are not. However, after adjusting for clinical confounders, dynamic RSI metrics do not independently predict antifungal treatment initiation. These findings suggest that serial CT monitoring and dynamic RSI assessment may reflect clinically meaningful disease progression, but current evidence does not support their use as standalone predictive tools for antifungal therapy decisions. Prospective studies with standardized imaging protocols are warranted to validate these exploratory results.

title: Do amikacin and colistin retain activity against carbapenem-resistant gram-negative bloodstream isolates in a single-center ICU?
abstract: BACKGROUND: Carbapenem-resistant Gram-negative bacilli (CR-GNB) bloodstream infections are increasingly encountered in intensive care units (ICUs) and remain associated with substantial mortality. In many regions, limited access to novel β-lactam/β-lactamase inhibitor (BL/BLI) agents has maintained the clinical relevance of older antibiotics such as amikacin and colistin. METHODS: This single-center retrospective study evaluated bloodstream infections caused by Gram-negative bacilli (GNB) in ICU patients, focusing on carbapenem resistance rates and susceptibility to amikacin and colistin. Bacterial identification and antimicrobial susceptibility testing were performed using standard microbiological methods, and resistance profiles were interpreted according to European Committee on Antimicrobial Susceptibility Testing (EUCAST) criteria. RESULTS: Among Gram-negative bloodstream isolates, 85.4% were carbapenem-resistant. Acinetobacter baumannii (94.5% resistant) and Klebsiella pneumoniae (92.6% resistant) were the predominant CR-GNB species, together accounting for more than 80% of resistant isolates. While amikacin showed moderate activity, particularly against K. pneumoniae, colistin showed some in vitro activity; however, given methodological limitations in susceptibility testing, these findings should be interpreted with caution. CONCLUSIONS: The high prevalence of carbapenem resistance in ICU bloodstream infections emphasizes the importance of initiating early appropriate antimicrobial therapy, guided by local resistance data. In settings with a high incidence of CR-GNB and restricted access to novel agents, these agents may be considered in selected cases, guided by local susceptibility data.

title: Unusual Presentation of Nasopharyngeal Mucormycosis: Case Report and Review of the Medical Literature.
abstract: Nasopharyngeal mucormycosis is exceptionally rare, with only three prior cases reported. We describe a 19-year-old male without prior medical illness who presented with progressive left ear pain that was initially managed as external otitis. Three weeks later, he developed diabetic ketoacidosis from newly diagnosed diabetes mellitus. During hospitalization, bilateral complete facial nerve paralysis (House-Brackmann grade 6) developed on consecutive days. Computed tomography showed only nasopharyngeal mucosal thickening, but direct nasopharyngoscopy revealed a necrotic mass. Histopathology confirmed acute invasive mucormycosis. The patient received liposomal amphotericin B for one month, underwent endoscopic debridement, and was discharged on oral posaconazole for two months. The fungal infection resolved completely, but the bilateral facial palsy showed no improvement. This case represents the fourth reported instance of nasopharyngeal mucormycosis and the first in a previously healthy young adult presenting with bilateral complete facial nerve palsy. The clinical course emphasizes that new-onset diabetic ketoacidosis alone can create sufficient susceptibility for invasive mucormycosis even in immunocompetent individuals. Furthermore, severe cranial neuropathy may precede any typical radiographic findings, making prompt endoscopic evaluation and empirical antifungal therapy critical. Despite successful infection eradication, neurological deficits can persist as permanent sequelae.

title: A Clinical Trial of Resistant Potato Starch for Gut MDRO Decolonization
sourceName: VA Office of Research and Development
abstract: Multidrug-resistant organisms (MDROs) cause serious infections that are difficult to treat, leading to increased morbidity and mortality, longer hospital stays, and increased healthcare costs. Many risk factors for MDRO infections are present in the Veteran population (such as older age, underlying medical conditions like diabetes, and stays in long-term healthcare settings). Some people can carry these organisms in their gut. Even without current symptoms, carrying these MDROs also increases risk of future infection. Effective, easy to use, and inexpensive interventions to reduce gut carriage of MDROs are needed to reduce risk of infection. Dietary fiber prebiotics have shown promise in improving the healthy gut microbiome, and the investigators have found that individuals with high fiber in their diets have reduced carriage of MDROs in the gut. The investigators propose a randomized controlled trial to test the effectiveness of a dietary fiber prebiotic intervention (resistant potato starch) in reducing gut MDRO carriage in Veterans with a history of MDRO carriage and/or infection. The investigators will also evaluate the effect on the gut microbiome as well as Veterans' experience with the fiber intervention.

title: Outbreak-driven dissemination of KPC variant-producing Klebsiella pneumoniae: the emerging challenge of ceftazidime/avibactam and cefiderocol co-resistance.
abstract: BACKGROUND: Ceftazidime/avibactam (CZA) resistance in KPC-producing Klebsiella pneumoniae is a critical public health threat, traditionally associated with in vivo selection. In this three-year study conducted in an Intensive Care Unit (ICU), we aimed to investigate the emergence of CZA-resistant (CZA-R) K. pneumoniae in patients treated with CZA, assessing the possible role of hospital outbreaks in dissemination. METHODS: We analysed a three-year dataset of antibiotic consumption and K. pneumoniae isolates collected from ICU patients receiving CZA therapy. Whole-genome sequencing (Illumina/Oxford Nanopore) and epidemiological reconstruction were used to investigate resistance mechanisms, KPC variants, and transmission dynamics, including outbreak detection. RESULTS: Among 871 ICU patients, 17.9% received CZA therapy, and 9% of these tested positive for CZA-resistant strains. We identified eight distinct KPC variants, including the novel KPC-295. While in vivo evolution remained the primary driver (71.4%), epidemiological reconstruction revealed that 28.6% of resistant isolates resulted from horizontal transmission, forming three distinct outbreaks of KPC-31, KPC-62, and KPC-66 producers. Alarmingly, 76.2% of CZA-R isolates exhibited co-resistance to FDC, a phenomenon linked to the presence of KPC variants conferring CZA resistance and likely enhanced by the fec operon. These clones persisted in the hospital environment and gut reservoirs of CZA-naive patients. CONCLUSIONS: Our findings suggest that CZA-R outbreaks may be underreported due to difficulties in KPC variant diagnostics and outbreak reconstruction. The emergence of co-resistance to CZA and FDC severely limits treatment options and poses major challenges for patient care and antimicrobial stewardship. These findings underscore the need for strengthened infection prevention and control measures, including early microbiological detection, active surveillance, and prompt containment strategies in ICU settings.

title: Challenges in monitoring and titration of argatroban versus unfractionated heparin in extracorporeal membrane oxygenation.
abstract: OBJECTIVES: Anticoagulation during extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (ECMO) remains challenging. Direct thrombin inhibitors such as argatroban are increasingly proposed as alternatives to unfractionated heparin (UFH). The primary outcome was the pooled proportion of measurements within the therapeutic target range. Secondary outcomes included dose requirements, time to target, dose-assay correlations, and platelet count trajectories. title: Global genomic surveillance and temporal trends of carbapenemase-encoding β-lactamase genes in Klebsiella pneumoniae using NCBI pathogen detection data.
abstract: The global spread of carbapenem-resistant Klebsiella pneumoniae is weakening the effectiveness of last-resort antibiotics and making severe infections increasingly difficult to treat. This study examined the geographical distribution, temporal patterns and co-occurrence of carbapenemase genes among K. pneumoniae genome assemblies deposited in the National Center for Biotechnology Information Pathogen Detection database. Genome metadata and antimicrobial resistance genotype information were retrieved between January and February 2026. After data cleaning, 67,057 unique genome assemblies from 123 countries contributed 77,975 carbapenemase-gene detections. Gene frequencies were summarised by continent, country, year and sample source. Poisson and negative binomial regression models were used to examine temporal patterns from 2013 to 2025. Genome-level co-occurrence was assessed using phi correlation coefficients, Jaccard similarity, odds ratios and Fisher's exact tests. blaKPC was the most frequently detected gene, with 39,832 detections (51.08%), followed by blaNDM with 24,412 (31.31%). blaNDM was the dominant gene in Africa, accounting for 1,101 detections (52.68%), whereas blaKPC was dominant in the Americas, Asia, Europe and Oceania, accounting for 59.29%, 56.50%, 38.37% and 38.77% of detections, respectively. Urine and blood were the main sample sources, representing approximately 30% and 22% of the analysed genomes, respectively. Yearly trend analysis showed increases in blaNDM, blaOXA-232 and blaOXA-181. The strongest negative association was found between blaKPC and blaNDM (φ = -0.69), although genomes carrying either gene frequently contained additional antimicrobial resistance genes. These findings demonstrate clear geographical and temporal differences in carbapenemase genes among genome assemblies deposited in NCBI pathogen detection. However, differences in sequencing capacity and database submissions across countries and years should be considered when interpreting the findings. Continued genomic surveillance, antimicrobial stewardship and stronger infection prevention and control measures are needed, particularly in underrepresented regions.

title: Fungal pneumonia in non-neutropenic critically ill patients: a Delphi consensus from the Fungal Infection Study Forum, India, with implications for resource-limited settings.
abstract: OBJECTIVES: To develop consensus-based, pragmatic recommendations for the diagnosis and management of fungal pneumonia in non-neutropenic critically ill adults in India and Asia, where the dual burden of mucormycosis and resource-limited healthcare settings creates distinct challenges. METHODS: Using a modified Delphi process, 20 multidisciplinary experts participated in the first round, and 19 completed the second and third rounds of anonymous voting on risk factors, diagnostic strategies, and management of invasive pulmonary aspergillosis (IPA), pulmonary mucormycosis (PM), and Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia (PCP). Consensus was defined as ≥ 70% agreement or disagreement; statements with 60-69% agreement were categorized as "suggest," while the remaining were classified as "no consensus." RESULTS: Key risk factors included severe chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, influenza, COVID-19, diabetes mellitus, and chronic liver or kidney disease. A multimodal diagnostic strategy combining contrast-enhanced computed tomography (CT), early bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL), microscopy, culture, and galactomannan (BAL threshold ≥ 1.0) was recommended, with molecular methods used where available. Liposomal amphotericin B was the preferred empiric agent in regions with high mucormycosis prevalence; voriconazole, posaconazole, or isavuconazole are first-line for proven IPA. Therapeutic drug monitoring is essential for azole antifungals, with a minimum treatment duration of 6-12 weeks. For PCP, empiric trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole is recommended in immunosuppressed patients with diffuse ground-glass opacities on CT after exclusion of competing diagnoses. Adjunctive corticosteroids are recommended for PCP with severe hypoxemia (PaO₂ <70 mmHg) despite limited evidence in non-HIV patients. CONCLUSION: We provide practical, resource-adapted guidance for managing fungal pneumonia in non-neutropenic ICU patients, while highlighting research priorities. The proposed diagnostic criteria for IPA and PM are provisional consensus-based frameworks intended to support clinical decision-making and require prospective multicentre validation. title: Direct Analysis in Real Time-Mass Spectrometry Measurement of Antifungals in Human Serum: A Proof-of-Concept Study.
sourceName: Journal of mass spectrometry and advances in the clinical lab
abstract: INTRODUCTION: Direct analysis in real time (DART) is a soft ionization technique that uses a heated gas such as helium, argon, or nitrogen to generate a cascade of ionized atmospheric molecules that subsequently ionize analytes in biological samples. OBJECTIVES: In this proof-of-concept study evaluating selected antifungals in human serum, 5-fluorocytosine (5FC), itraconazole (ITR), hydroxyitraconazole (OH-ITR), isavuconazole (ISV), ketoconazole (KETO), fluconazole (FLU), and posaconazole (POSA) were assessed as DART candidates using a Bruker EVOQ® DART-TQ+. METHODS: Human serum samples were extracted using protein precipitation or liquid-liquid extraction. Quantification was performed by DART tandem mass spectrometry (DART-MS/MS) with internal standards. Precision and linearity across individual analytical measurement ranges (AMRs) were evaluated with rapid sample acquisition (0.24 min linear scans), and the results were compared with those obtained using validated LC-MS/MS methods. RESULTS: Linearity and precision were acceptable for all evaluated compounds. Good agreement with LC-MS/MS was observed for 5FC, ITR, OH-ITR, and FLU, with slopes ranging from 0.875 to 1.112 and correlation coefficients ( CONCLUSION: This proof-of-concept study demonstrates the feasibility of quantitative antifungal measurement in human serum using DART-MS/MS with simple sample preparation. A moderate linear association with bias for POSA was likely attributable to matrix effects. More selective sample preparation may improve DART accuracy. Overall, DART-MS/MS shows promise as a rapid, high-throughput alternative to conventional LC-MS/MS. Researchers tested a fast mass spectrometry technique (direct analysis in real time tandem mass spectrometry, DART-MS/MS) to measure antifungal drugs in human blood serum. Using simple extraction steps, they analyzed seven common medications and compared the results with those obtained using a standard liquid chromatography tandem mass spectrometry (LC-MS/MS) lab method. For most drugs, accuracy, precision, and linearity were good and matched those of the reference method. Posaconazole showed some bias, likely from sample matrix effects. Overall, DART-MS/MS appears promising for quick, high-throughput drug level monitoring.
